text: Did the man die as a result of a fall from an aircraft?
Was the man a passenger on a hot-air balloon that was losing altitude?
Were the suitcases thrown out of the balloon to lighten it, and did the man fall or jump out as part of that same attempt to save the balloon?
Did the man fall or jump from the balloon himself (rather than being thrown out with the suitcases)?
Was the man already dead before he left the balloon?
Was the balloon losing altitude, and did the people in it throw out the suitcases and also throw the man out to lighten the load, causing him to fall to his death?
Did the man die because the balloon crashed or landed while he was still alive in it, rather than by falling from it?
Was the man in the balloon because he was a pilot or crew member rather than a passenger?
Was the man still holding onto or attached to something from the balloon (such as a rope or part of the basket) as he fell, so that he was not simply thrown clear?
Did the man fall from the balloon because the balloon's basket or structure gave way beneath him while he was in it?
Did the people in the balloon draw lots (using matchsticks) to decide who would jump out to lighten the balloon?
Did the man draw the short half-matchstick, meaning he was chosen as the one to jump out?
Did the men in the balloon agree that whoever drew the shorter matchstick would jump out of the balloon?
Was the man chosen by the matchstick draw to jump, but he refused or failed to jump, so someone else threw him out?
Were the matchsticks used to determine which of several people would be the one to leave the balloon, and did the man end up being the one who had to leave?
Was the man the one who was supposed to jump out of the balloon, and did someone else in the balloon go with him or follow him out?
Did the man jump out of the balloon voluntarily after losing the matchstick draw?

The man was a passenger in a hot-air balloon that was losing altitude over the desert. To lighten it, the people aboard threw out several suitcases. They then used matchsticks to draw lots to decide who among them would jump out; the man drew the short half-matchstick, meaning he was the one required to leave. He did not jump voluntarily, so the other occupants forced or threw him out of the balloon. He fell from the balloon into the desert and died on impact, still clutching the half matchstick that had marked him as the chosen sacrifice.
